Same formula. Pro's twelve-month cancellation figure is 40%, so 1 / 0.40 = 2.5. Check: 0.40 × 2.5 = 1.00. So 2.5 years of expected life, which is 30 months.

Then LTV = 30 months × $80 monthly margin = $2,400. CAC is $1,200, so the ratio is $2,400 / $1,200 = 2.0.

So Pro sits below the board's three-times bar while Starter sits above it. That's the opposite of what the CFO is claiming, and it's worth pressure-testing before we go further — the gap is driven mostly by the CAC difference, $1,200 for a salesperson-led demo versus $300 self-serve. Pro would need either a materially cheaper sales motion or a longer life to clear 3x.

One thing I'd want: do we know how Pro's CAC has moved since January 2025? If the sales team is now chasing fewer Pro deals, $1,200 may be rising.

turnRows.text:
Our client is Quillpath, a US software company. It sells cloud software that small home-services businesses — plumbers, landscapers, cleaners — use to schedule jobs, send quotes and get paid. Customers pay monthly and can cancel at any time. For years Quillpath sold one plan, Pro, at $100 a month. In January 2025 it launched a cheaper Starter plan at $40 a month, with fewer features and a single user. New customers per month nearly tripled. Quillpath's board has a rule: each type of customer should be worth at least three times what it costs to acquire. The CFO says Starter fails that test and wants to shut it down; the head of growth wants to keep it. The CEO has asked us what Quillpath should do with the Starter plan.

How would you like to approach this? Feel free to take a moment to gather your thoughts first.

Let me lay out how I'd attack this. The board rule is basically an LTV-to-CAC test, so I'd break it into three buckets.

First, the value side for Starter: what a Starter customer pays per month, and how long they stay — so monthly revenue times gross margin times expected lifetime, which is driven by the churn rate.

Second, the cost side: what it costs to acquire a Starter customer — sales and marketing spend per new Starter signup. Starter is self-serve-ish presumably, so CAC might be lower than Pro's.

Third, the cross-effects the CFO might be missing: do Starter customers upgrade to Pro over time, and is Starter cannibalizing Pro signups that would have come anyway?

Could I start with the value side — do we have the churn rates and the CAC for each plan?

Understood. I'll come back to churn rates and CAC for each plan shortly. Before any data: your structure covers Starter's own LTV-to-CAC and the cross-effects with Pro. Is that MECE, or is something missing from how you'd answer the CEO's question about what to do with the plan?

Fair push — I think I'm missing two things.

One, cost to serve, not just cost to acquire. Starter customers still file support tickets and consume hosting; if a $40 customer costs nearly as much to support as a $100 one, that crushes the margin and the LTV side. So I'd want gross margin by plan, not just revenue.

Two, my structure implicitly frames this as keep-or-kill, which is binary. The real answer space is wider: reprice Starter, change the feature gating so upgrading to Pro is more attractive, shift the acquisition mix to cheaper channels to lower CAC, or limit Starter to segments where it doesn't cannibalize. Shutting down is just one branch.

So: Starter economics, cross-effects on Pro, cost to serve, and then the menu of actions. Can we start with churn and CAC by plan?

Right, a wider action menu. On what you asked about earlier: Of the 1,050 Pro customers who signed up in January–March 2025, 98.0% were still on Pro after month 1, 94.1% after month 3, 88.6% after month 6 and 78.5% after month 12, so 2.0%, 5.9%, 11.4% and 21.5% had cancelled by those months. Of the 3,000 Starter customers who signed up in January–March 2025, 94% were still on Starter after month 1, 82% after month 3, 65% after month 6 and 40% after month 12; by those months 1%, 5%, 11% and 20% had upgraded to Pro and were still customers, and 5%, 13%, 24% and 40% had cancelled. Here's an exhibit: Quillpath — Economics of each plan ($ per customer). With those figures in front of you, how would you use them to test Starter against the board's three-times rule?

Let me work the lifetime first, then multiply by margin.

Margins per month: Pro is $100 − $20 = $80. Starter is $40 − $10 = $30.

For Starter, the churn figure I'll use is 21.5% — that's the clean cancellation rate we have. Average lifetime is roughly 1 divided by churn, so 1 / 0.215 ≈ 4.65 months. LTV = 4.65 × $30 ≈ $140. Against a $300 CAC that's a ratio of about 0.47 — well under 3. So the CFO is right that it fails, and it fails badly, not marginally.

For Pro, the comparable cancellation figure is 40%, so lifetime ≈ 1 / 0.40 = 2.5 months, LTV = 2.5 × $80 = $200 against $1,200 CAC — ratio 0.17.

That's striking: on these numbers Pro looks worse than Starter, which flips the CFO's argument.

Do we have monthly new-signup counts by plan since launch, so I can see if the mix is still shifting?

Mm-hm. An exhibit for you — Quillpath — New customers per month, by plan (average per month). Before we go there: you used 21.5% for Starter and 40% for Pro. Walk me through where each of those came from in the cohort data.

Sure. 21.5% is the twelve-month cancellation figure from the Starter cohort — it's the cleanest full-year read we have, so I used it as the annual churn for Starter. And 40% is the corresponding twelve-month cancellation number on the Pro side, so I used that for Pro.

I'll flag one thing I glossed over: those are twelve-month cumulative figures, and I divided one into them as if they were monthly rates. If I treat them as annual instead, Starter's lifetime is about 1 / 0.215 ≈ 4.65 years, so LTV ≈ 4.65 × 12 × $30 ≈ $1,675 against $300 CAC — a ratio over 5. And Pro at 1 / 0.40 = 2.5 years gives 2.5 × 12 × $80 = $2,400 against $1,200, a ratio of 2.0.

On that reading Starter passes the three-times rule comfortably and Pro is the plan that fails. Either way, Starter beats Pro.
Right, you caught the monthly versus annual mix-up yourself. You said “4.65” — what were the steps in that calculation?

Yes — it's the standard lifetime approximation: if a fixed fraction of customers cancels each period, average lifetime is 1 divided by that fraction. So for Starter, 1 / 0.215 = 4.65. The arithmetic: 0.215 × 4 = 0.86, 0.215 × 4.65 ≈ 1.00, so 4.65 periods. Since 21.5% is the twelve-month cancellation figure, the period is a year, so 4.65 years, or about 56 months.

Same method for Pro: 1 / 0.40 = 2.5 years, 30 months.

I'd caveat that the approximation assumes a constant rate, and the Starter cohort data isn't constant — cancellations are front-loaded, 5% in month 1 alone. So the true lifetime is probably shorter than 4.65 years. But directionally Starter still clears 3x with a lot of room, and Pro at 2.0x is the one in trouble.
Understood. You mentioned “2.5” — take me through the math there.
